questions.question: Q1. Define linear momentum and state its SI unit.
questions.answer: Linear momentum is the product of mass and velocity, p = mv. SI unit = kg m s⁻¹ (vector, same direction as v).
questions.example: 1000 kg car at 20 m/s → p = 20000 kg·m/s.

questions.question: Q2. Define impulse and relate it to momentum.
questions.answer: Impulse is the product of the force and the time for which it acts, J = Ft. By impulse-momentum theorem, impulse equals the change in momentum: J = Δp = FΔt.
questions.shortcut: J = FΔt = Δp (area under F-t graph).
questions.example: A 5 N force for 0.4 s → J = 2 N·s (momentum change).

questions.question: Q3. State Newton's second law in its general form.
questions.answer: The net external force equals the rate of change of momentum: F = dp/dt. For constant mass, F = ma. ▥ 4.1 Linear Momentum & Impulse  —  Compare / Contrast Tables Momentum vs Impulse ▣ 4.2 Conservation of Linear Momentum
questions.shortcut: F = dp/dt; if m const, F = ma.

questions.question: Q4. State the law of conservation of momentum.
questions.answer: If the net external force on a system is zero, the total linear momentum of the system remains constant: Σp_before = Σp_after.
questions.example: A gun recoils when it fires (both momenta equal and opposite).

questions.question: Q5. A 2 kg and a 3 kg body collide and stick; before: 2 kg at 6 m/s, 3 kg at rest. Find common velocity.
questions.example: The combined body moves at 2.4 m/s.

questions.question: Q6. Explain recoil of a gun using conservation of momentum.
questions.answer: Initially total momentum is zero. After firing, bullet (mass m, speed v) gains forward momentum mv; the gun (M) recoils with momentum MV backward, so mv = MV, V = mv/M. ▥ 4.2 Conservation of Linear Momentum  —  Compare / Contrast Tables When is Linear Momentum Conserved? ▣ 4.3 Application of Newton's Laws
questions.shortcut: V_recoil = (bullet m / gun M) × bullet v.
questions.example: M=5 kg, m=0.05 kg, v=200 m/s → V = 2 m/s backward.

questions.question: Q7. State Newton's third law and give two applications.
questions.answer: To every action there is an equal and opposite reaction; the forces act on different bodies. Applications: walking (foot pushes ground), propulsion of a rocket, gun recoil.
questions.shortcut: Action and reaction are on different bodies, never cancel each other.
questions.example: A rocket expels gas backward; gas pushes rocket forward.

questions.question: Q8. A 10 kg body is pulled on a rough surface by a 50 N horizontal force, μ=0.2. Find acceleration.
Q9. Explain why a rider leans while taking a turn.
questions.answer: To balance the centripetal force, the rider leans so that the resultant of weight and normal reaction passes through the centre; the horizontal component of the normal reaction provides the required centripetal force. ▥ 4.3 Application of Newton's Laws  —  Compare / Contrast Tables Newton's Laws: Apparent Weight in a Lift ▣ 4.4 Moment, Torque & Equilibrium
questions.shortcut: Tilt to supply horizontal centripetal component.
questions.example: Bicycle rider leans into the curve.

questions.question: Q10. Define moment (torque) and its SI unit.
questions.answer: Moment of a force about a point is the product of the force and the perpendicular distance of its line of action from the point: τ = rF. SI unit = N·m.
questions.example: A 5 N force 0.3 m from a pivot → τ = 1.5 N·m.

questions.question: Q11. State the conditions for a body to be in equilibrium.
questions.answer: (i) Translational equilibrium: ΣF = 0. (ii) Rotational equilibrium: Στ = 0 about any point.
questions.shortcut: Both forces and moments must balance.
questions.example: A balanced see-saw satisfies both conditions.

questions.question: Q12. Explain the principle of moments and its use in a lever.
questions.answer: For rotational equilibrium, the algebraic sum of clockwise moments equals the sum of anticlockwise moments about any point. In a lever this lets a small force at a long arm balance a large force at a short arm. ▥ 4.4 Moment, Torque & Equilibrium  —  Compare / Contrast Tables Translational vs Rotational: Quantity Pairs ▣ 4.5 Solid Friction
questions.example: A seesaw balances when F₁d₁ = F₂d₂.

questions.question: Q13. State the laws of solid friction.
questions.answer: (i) Friction is proportional to the normal reaction (f ∝ N). (ii) It is independent of the area of contact. (iii) It is independent of sliding velocity (roughly). (iv) It depends on the nature of surfaces. (v) Limiting friction > sliding friction.
questions.shortcut: f = μN; μ_k < μ_s; independent of area & speed.
questions.example: Heavy object is harder to slide (larger N → larger f).

questions.question: Q14. Distinguish static, limiting and dynamic (kinetic) friction.
questions.answer: Static friction acts when bodies are at rest (self-adjusts up to a maximum). Limiting friction is the maximum static friction just before motion. Dynamic friction acts during sliding and is slightly less than limiting.
questions.shortcut: Rest → static; threshold → limiting; sliding → kinetic (< limiting).
questions.example: You must push harder to start sliding than to keep sliding.

questions.question: Q15. A 15 kg block on a horizontal floor, μ_s=0.4. Minimum force to start motion?
questions.answer: Limiting friction = μ_s mg = 0.4×15×9.8 = 58.8 N. A horizontal force just above 58.8 N starts motion.

questions.question: Q16. Why is the coefficient of kinetic friction less than that of static friction?
questions.answer: When surfaces are at rest the microscopic irregularities interlock, requiring more force to break; once sliding, the interlock is partially broken and fewer asperities engage, so kinetic friction is lower. ▥ 4.5 Solid Friction  —  Compare / Contrast Tables Static vs Kinetic vs Rolling Friction PROFESSOR'S THEORY & VIVA BANK   — the kinds of theory a professor / examiner actually asks
questions.shortcut: μ_k < μ_s due to broken interlocking asperities.
questions.example: Starting a load is harder than keeping it moving.

theoryItems.question: [Derive] T1. Derive the impulse-momentum theorem.
theoryItems.answer: F = dp/dt → FΔt = Δp (constant mass: Ft = m(v−u)). The impulse Ft equals the change in momentum; graphically it is the area under the F–t curve.
theoryItems.example: A cushiony landing spreads force over more time → smaller F.

theoryItems.question: [Derive] T2. Derive the expression for the recoil velocity of a gun.
theoryItems.answer: Initial momentum zero. After firing: mv_bullet = MV_gun (opposite directions) → V_gun = (m/M)v_bullet.
theoryItems.example: Gun is much heavier → small recoil velocity.

theoryItems.question: [State] T3. State Newton's three laws of motion.
theoryItems.answer: I: body stays at rest/uniform motion unless a net force acts (inertia). II: F = dp/dt (= ma for constant mass). III: to every action an equal and opposite reaction (on different bodies).
theoryItems.shortcut: I inertia; II F=ma; III action-reaction.
theoryItems.example: A book stays put until pushed; it accelerates when pushed.

theoryItems.question: [State] T4. State the conditions for equilibrium (translational and rotational).
theoryItems.answer: Translational: ΣF = 0 (no linear acceleration). Rotational: Στ about any point = 0 (no angular acceleration). Both must hold for a body to be in complete static equilibrium.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T5. Explain the concept of inertia and its dependence on mass.
theoryItems.answer: Inertia is the tendency of a body to resist changes in its state of motion; it is measured by mass (larger mass → more inertia). This is the content of the first law.
theoryItems.example: A loaded truck is harder to stop than a bicycle.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T6. Explain the conservation of linear momentum with an example.
theoryItems.answer: If the net external force on a system is zero, total momentum stays constant. In a collision: m₁v₁ + m₂v₂ = m₁v₁′ + m₂v₂′. Example: recoil of a gun (momentum of bullet = that of gun, opposite).

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T7. Explain moment of a force and torque with an example.
theoryItems.answer: Moment (torque) of a force about a point = force × perpendicular distance from the point: τ = rF sinθ. It measures the turning effect; SI unit N·m. A spanner: longer handle → larger τ for the same force.
theoryItems.example: Longer lever arm = easier to open a jar.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T8. Explain the laws of solid friction and their verification.
theoryItems.answer: (i) f ∝ N (µ constant); (ii) independent of area of contact; (iii) independent of sliding speed; (iv) depend on the nature of surfaces; (v) limiting friction > kinetic friction. Verified by pulling a block on an inclined plane / horizontal, plotting f vs N (straight line through origin).
theoryItems.shortcut: f = µN ; verify by f–N plot.

theoryItems.question: [Viva] T9. Professor: 'Why is it harder to start a heavy crate moving than to keep it moving?'
theoryItems.answer: Because limiting (static) friction is larger than kinetic (dynamic) friction; the interlocked surface asperities resist the start. Once sliding, fewer asperities engage → lower friction.
theoryItems.shortcut: µ_s > µ_k → start needs more force.
theoryItems.example: This is why you 'break the static' then it eases.

theoryItems.question: [Numerical] T10. A 4 kg block is pulled by 30 N on a rough floor, µ=0.2, g=10. Find the friction and acceleration.
theoryItems.answer: N = mg = 40 N. Friction f = µN = 8 N. Net = 30−8 = 22 N. a = 22/4 = 5.5 m/s².

UNIT 4: DYNAMICS   Content Area: Mechanics
All-possible NEB questions  •  short precise answers  •  exam shortcuts  •  worked examples
▣ 4.1 Linear Momentum & Impulse
Q1. Define linear momentum and state its SI unit.
Answer:  Linear momentum is the product of mass and velocity, p = mv. SI unit = kg m s⁻¹ (vector, same direction as v).
⚡ Shortcut:  p = mv (vector).
Example:  1000 kg car at 20 m/s → p = 20000 kg·m/s.
Q2. Define impulse and relate it to momentum.
Answer:  Impulse is the product of the force and the time for which it acts, J = Ft. By impulse-momentum theorem, impulse equals the change in momentum: J = Δp = FΔt.
⚡ Shortcut:  J = FΔt = Δp (area under F-t graph).
Example:  A 5 N force for 0.4 s → J = 2 N·s (momentum change).
Q3. State Newton's second law in its general form.
Answer:  The net external force equals the rate of change of momentum: F = dp/dt. For constant mass, F = ma.
⚡ Shortcut:  F = dp/dt; if m const, F = ma.
Example:  Faster momentum change → larger force.
▥ 4.1 Linear Momentum & Impulse  —  Compare / Contrast Tables
Momentum vs Impulse
▣ 4.2 Conservation of Linear Momentum
Q4. State the law of conservation of momentum.
Answer:  If the net external force on a system is zero, the total linear momentum of the system remains constant: Σp_before = Σp_after.
⚡ Shortcut:  No external force → m₁v₁+m₂v₂ = m₁v₁′+m₂v₂′.
Example:  A gun recoils when it fires (both momenta equal and opposite).
Q5. A 2 kg and a 3 kg body collide and stick; before: 2 kg at 6 m/s, 3 kg at rest. Find common velocity.
Answer:  Perfectly inelastic: m₁v₁+m₂v₂ = (m₁+m₂)v → 2×6+3×0 = 5v → v = 12/5 = 2.4 m/s.
⚡ Shortcut:  Stick together → v = m₁v₁/(m₁+m₂).
Example:  The combined body moves at 2.4 m/s.
Q6. Explain recoil of a gun using conservation of momentum.
Answer:  Initially total momentum is zero. After firing, bullet (mass m, speed v) gains forward momentum mv; the gun (M) recoils with momentum MV backward, so mv = MV, V = mv/M.
⚡ Shortcut:  V_recoil = (bullet m / gun M) × bullet v.
Example:  M=5 kg, m=0.05 kg, v=200 m/s → V = 2 m/s backward.
▥ 4.2 Conservation of Linear Momentum  —  Compare / Contrast Tables
When is Linear Momentum Conserved?
▣ 4.3 Application of Newton's Laws
Q7. State Newton's third law and give two applications.
Answer:  To every action there is an equal and opposite reaction; the forces act on different bodies. Applications: walking (foot pushes ground), propulsion of a rocket, gun recoil.
⚡ Shortcut:  Action and reaction are on different bodies, never cancel each other.
Example:  A rocket expels gas backward; gas pushes rocket forward.
Q8. A 10 kg body is pulled on a rough surface by a 50 N horizontal force, μ=0.2. Find acceleration.
Answer:  N = mg = 98 N; friction f = μN = 19.6 N. Net = 50−19.6 = 30.4 N; a = 30.4/10 = 3.04 m/s².
⚡ Shortcut:  a = (F − μmg)/m.
Example:  ≈ 3 m/s².
Q9. Explain why a rider leans while taking a turn.

Answer:  To balance the centripetal force, the rider leans so that the resultant of weight and normal reaction passes through the centre; the horizontal component of the normal reaction provides the required centripetal force.
⚡ Shortcut:  Tilt to supply horizontal centripetal component.
Example:  Bicycle rider leans into the curve.
▥ 4.3 Application of Newton's Laws  —  Compare / Contrast Tables
Newton's Laws: Apparent Weight in a Lift
▣ 4.4 Moment, Torque & Equilibrium
Q10. Define moment (torque) and its SI unit.
Answer:  Moment of a force about a point is the product of the force and the perpendicular distance of its line of action from the point: τ = rF. SI unit = N·m.
⚡ Shortcut:  τ = r × F (perpendicular distance only).
Example:  A 5 N force 0.3 m from a pivot → τ = 1.5 N·m.
Q11. State the conditions for a body to be in equilibrium.
Answer:  (i) Translational equilibrium: ΣF = 0. (ii) Rotational equilibrium: Στ = 0 about any point.
⚡ Shortcut:  Both forces and moments must balance.
Example:  A balanced see-saw satisfies both conditions.
Q12. Explain the principle of moments and its use in a lever.

Answer:  For rotational equilibrium, the algebraic sum of clockwise moments equals the sum of anticlockwise moments about any point. In a lever this lets a small force at a long arm balance a large force at a short arm.
⚡ Shortcut:  Σ(M_clockwise)=Σ(M_anticlockwise); lever: F×d = W×d′.
Example:  A seesaw balances when F₁d₁ = F₂d₂.
▥ 4.4 Moment, Torque & Equilibrium  —  Compare / Contrast Tables
Translational vs Rotational: Quantity Pairs
▣ 4.5 Solid Friction
Q13. State the laws of solid friction.

Answer:  (i) Friction is proportional to the normal reaction (f ∝ N). (ii) It is independent of the area of contact. (iii) It is independent of sliding velocity (roughly). (iv) It depends on the nature of surfaces. (v) Limiting friction > sliding friction.
⚡ Shortcut:  f = μN; μ_k < μ_s; independent of area & speed.
Example:  Heavy object is harder to slide (larger N → larger f).
Q14. Distinguish static, limiting and dynamic (kinetic) friction.

Answer:  Static friction acts when bodies are at rest (self-adjusts up to a maximum). Limiting friction is the maximum static friction just before motion. Dynamic friction acts during sliding and is slightly less than limiting.
⚡ Shortcut:  Rest → static; threshold → limiting; sliding → kinetic (< limiting).
Example:  You must push harder to start sliding than to keep sliding.
Q15. A 15 kg block on a horizontal floor, μ_s=0.4. Minimum force to start motion?
Answer:  Limiting friction = μ_s mg = 0.4×15×9.8 = 58.8 N. A horizontal force just above 58.8 N starts motion.
⚡ Shortcut:  F_min = μ_s mg.
Example:  ≈ 59 N.
Q16. Why is the coefficient of kinetic friction less than that of static friction?

Answer:  When surfaces are at rest the microscopic irregularities interlock, requiring more force to break; once sliding, the interlock is partially broken and fewer asperities engage, so kinetic friction is lower.
⚡ Shortcut:  μ_k < μ_s due to broken interlocking asperities.
Example:  Starting a load is harder than keeping it moving.
▥ 4.5 Solid Friction  —  Compare / Contrast Tables
Static vs Kinetic vs Rolling Friction
PROFESSOR'S THEORY & VIVA BANK   — the kinds of theory a professor / examiner actually asks
▹ Derive  (derivations & long answers)
[Derive] T1. Derive the impulse-momentum theorem.
Answer:  F = dp/dt → FΔt = Δp (constant mass: Ft = m(v−u)). The impulse Ft equals the change in momentum; graphically it is the area under the F–t curve.
⚡ Short / exam line:  J = FΔt = Δp.
Example:  A cushiony landing spreads force over more time → smaller F.
[Derive] T2. Derive the expression for the recoil velocity of a gun.
Answer:  Initial momentum zero. After firing: mv_bullet = MV_gun (opposite directions) → V_gun = (m/M)v_bullet.
⚡ Short / exam line:  V = (bullet m / gun M)·v_bullet.
Example:  Gun is much heavier → small recoil velocity.
▹ State  (definitions, laws & formulae)
[State] T3. State Newton's three laws of motion.
Answer:  I: body stays at rest/uniform motion unless a net force acts (inertia). II: F = dp/dt (= ma for constant mass). III: to every action an equal and opposite reaction (on different bodies).
⚡ Short / exam line:  I inertia; II F=ma; III action-reaction.
Example:  A book stays put until pushed; it accelerates when pushed.
[State] T4. State the conditions for equilibrium (translational and rotational).
Answer:  Translational: ΣF = 0 (no linear acceleration). Rotational: Στ about any point = 0 (no angular acceleration). Both must hold for a body to be in complete static equilibrium.
⚡ Short / exam line:  ΣF=0 and Στ=0.
Example:  A balanced see-saw satisfies both.
▹ Explain  (working / principle / application)
[Explain] T5. Explain the concept of inertia and its dependence on mass.
Answer:  Inertia is the tendency of a body to resist changes in its state of motion; it is measured by mass (larger mass → more inertia). This is the content of the first law.
⚡ Short / exam line:  Inertia ∝ mass (resistance to change).
Example:  A loaded truck is harder to stop than a bicycle.
[Explain] T6. Explain the conservation of linear momentum with an example.

Answer:  If the net external force on a system is zero, total momentum stays constant. In a collision: m₁v₁ + m₂v₂ = m₁v₁′ + m₂v₂′. Example: recoil of a gun (momentum of bullet = that of gun, opposite).
⚡ Short / exam line:  ΣF_ext = 0 → Σp constant.
Example:  Muzzle: mv_bullet = MV_gun.
[Explain] T7. Explain moment of a force and torque with an example.

Answer:  Moment (torque) of a force about a point = force × perpendicular distance from the point: τ = rF sinθ. It measures the turning effect; SI unit N·m. A spanner: longer handle → larger τ for the same force.
⚡ Short / exam line:  τ = r F⊥ ; unit N·m.
Example:  Longer lever arm = easier to open a jar.
[Explain] T8. Explain the laws of solid friction and their verification.

Answer:  (i) f ∝ N (µ constant); (ii) independent of area of contact; (iii) independent of sliding speed; (iv) depend on the nature of surfaces; (v) limiting friction > kinetic friction. Verified by pulling a block on an inclined plane / horizontal, plotting f vs N (straight line through origin).
⚡ Short / exam line:  f = µN ; verify by f–N plot.
Example:  Heavier block → larger friction (f ∝ N).
▹ Viva  (viva-voce probing)
[Viva] T9. Professor: 'Why is it harder to start a heavy crate moving than to keep it moving?'
Answer:  Because limiting (static) friction is larger than kinetic (dynamic) friction; the interlocked surface asperities resist the start. Once sliding, fewer asperities engage → lower friction.
⚡ Short / exam line:  µ_s > µ_k → start needs more force.
Example:  This is why you 'break the static' then it eases.
▹ Numerical  (long numericals / problems)
[Numerical] T10. A 4 kg block is pulled by 30 N on a rough floor, µ=0.2, g=10. Find the friction and acceleration.
Answer:  N = mg = 40 N. Friction f = µN = 8 N. Net = 30−8 = 22 N. a = 22/4 = 5.5 m/s².
⚡ Short / exam line:  f=µN; a=(F−f)/m.
Example:  ≈ 5.5 m/s².
